stimulus.text: The resistance to British taxes was not only the work of famous leaders. In 1774, fifty-one women in Edenton, North Carolina, signed a declaration vowing to give up tea and other British products. Across the colonies, women organized spinning bees to make homespun cloth, replacing British imports. In Boston, shoemaker Ebenezer Macintosh led crowd actions against Stamp Act officials, and artisans who backed the boycotts found new demand for American-made goods.

books.section: B. The Resistance Movement from Above and from Below

stem: The actions described in the passage most directly show that colonial resistance...

options.text: Was led entirely by wealthy merchants and lawyers
options.misconception: The passage is about women and artisans, not merchants and lawyers — the point is that resistance reached beyond the elite.

options.text: Depended on British troops to enforce the boycotts
options.misconception: British troops enforced British laws, not colonial boycotts — the boycotts were enforced by colonial committees and by the women and artisans themselves.

options.text: Reached beyond political leaders to include women and artisans
Ended as soon as the Stamp Act was repealed
options.misconception: The passage includes the Edenton Tea Party of 1774 — eight years after the Stamp Act's repeal — so resistance clearly did not end in 1766.

rationales.C: The passage names the actors: fifty-one women in Edenton, women spinning homespun, a Boston shoemaker leading crowds. Resistance was not only the work of famous leaders — it reached into households and workshops.
rationales.A: Merchants and lawyers are not the actors here. The passage is about women and artisans.
rationales.B: The troops were on the other side. Boycotts were enforced by colonial committees, not by British soldiers.
rationales.D: The Edenton declaration is dated 1774 — eight years after repeal. Resistance outlived the Stamp Act.
rationales.general:
1. List who acts in the passage. Women signing declarations, women spinning cloth, a shoemaker leading crowds — not governors or generals.
2. Ask what that list proves. Resistance reached beyond the men who wrote the petitions, into households and workshops.
3. Ask why that mattered. A boycott works only if ordinary buyers refuse to buy — and the buyers were women, the makers were artisans.
Remember: a movement is measured by who joins it, not just by who leads it — count the crowd, not only the captains.
